newsitem.title: UK: Aspirin helps prevent new strokes, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Aspirin helps prevent new strokes, study finds.

text.p: Aspirin, that old reliable standby used to treat everything from headaches to heart attacks, can also help prevent stroke, researchers said on Friday.
They recommended that aspirin be given immediately to people who have suffered ischaemic strokes -- the kind caused by blood clots.

But other experts called the findings inconclusive even though there is no suggestion that giving aspirin could do any harm. Some concern has emerged that aspirin, which can cause internal bleeding, could be harmful to stroke victims.

Two trials of 40,000 stroke patients -- one an international collaboration involving 36 countries and one based in China -- found aspirin slightly decreased the rate of death in the first two weeks after a stroke.
"Doctors already knew that long-term aspirin use is helpful," said Peter Sandercock of the University of Edinburgh, who helped coordinate the international trial of 20,000 patients.
"Now we've shown that doctors shouldn't be afraid to start giving patients aspirin immediately."
He added: "It's good to find the cheapest, easiest treatment is the best."
The study, published in the Lancet medical journal,compared aspirin with heparin, another drug used to help prevent blood clots. It found heparin slightly increased the risk of haemorrhagic stroke.
Marie-Germaine Bousser, a neurologist at the Hopital Saint-Antoine in Paris, called the results "somewhat disappointing" and said aspirin was not necessarily safe in all cases after stroke.
Nor was the Lancet itself impressed. "Neither patients nor clinicians will find in this week's issue of the Lancet a breakthrough in therapy," it said in an editorial.
"It took a study of 20,000 patients to come up with a cautionary note on the role of heparin in treatment and no clear-cut positive message about aspirin."
